name: Loan
seoDesc: Loan: work out loan amount fee from the interest rate and the periodic payment. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Loan calculator the interest rate, the periodic payment, the loan term and the prepaid fee and it returns loan amount fee. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Loan calculator work?
sections.html:
The Loan calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports loan amount fee in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the compound frequency and the origination fee repayment); then you type in the interest rate, the periodic payment, the loan term and the prepaid fee.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Loan calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Fee amount=origination fee × loan amount
Ir=(what interest rate do you know?, annual Percentage Rate (APR), interest rate)
Eq p=(((M + (what interest rate do you know?, annual Percentage Rate (APR), interest rate)) ÷ M, M ÷ payment frequency) − 1)
Payment frequency=periods ÷ loan term
Loaned fee Fee_rolled=(what interest rate do you know?, origination fee repayment, interest rate, annual Percentage Rate (APR), fee amount, loaned fee)
Payment 2=(loan amount, (loan amount − (origination fee × loan amount)), (((M + (what interest rate do you know?, annual Percentage Rate (APR), interest rate)) ÷ M, M ÷ payment frequency) − 1), periods, (what interest rate do you know?, origination fee repayment, interest rate, annual Percentage Rate (APR), fee amount, loaned fee), origination fee repayment, what interest rate do you know?, fee amount, (loan amount, (what interest rate do you know?, origination fee repayment, interest rate, annual Percentage Rate (APR), fee amount, loaned fee), what interest rate do you know?), interest rate, annual Percentage Rate (APR), M, payment frequency)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Loan calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the interest rate, the periodic payment and the loan term — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Loan calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns loan amount fee, derived from the interest rate, the periodic payment and the loan term. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Loan calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the interest rate, the periodic payment, the loan term and the prepaid fee, which is 15 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter interest rate in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Interest rate opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Loan calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
